Reproductive biology in the Damaraland mole-rat (Cryptomys damarensis) is characterized by a singular breeding female within each colony, a pattern known as reproductive skew. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their subterranean burrows, maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of this species translates into a modest output of approximately 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 3 pups per litter] and up to 4 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 4 litters per year], yielding roughly 12 pups per year [Ri = roughly 12 pups per year]. This low annual fecundity is a hallmark of cooperative breeders, where the non-breeding colony members assist in rearing the offspring. The gestation period, which lasts 93 days [tg = 93 days], is notably prolonged for a rodent of this size and is recorded when the female is kept at a core body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This extended gestation likely reflects the constraints of a low metabolic rate combined with the energetic demands of producing a relatively well-developed altricial pup. Field observations of the sole reproductive female within a group reveal that she can successfully rear only a few litters each year, constrained by the limited capacity of her helpers to provision the young.

Following the lengthy gestation, the neonatal pup emerges at a remarkably small size. At birth, the wet weight of a newborn is merely 9 grams [Wwb = 9 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the offspring. This tiny mass, equivalent to only a small fraction of the mother's body weight, is a common life-history trait among subterranean rodents that produce a single, heavily invested litter at a time. The newborn pup is entirely dependent on the colony for warmth and nutrition. This weaning age, observed at a burrow temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], marks a critical transition where the juvenile begins to consume the same fibrous geophytes as the adults, although it continues to receive some nutritional support from colony members. The rapid weaning is an adaptation to reduce the energetic burden on the lactating queen and allows the colony's resources to be directed toward the next reproductive cycle.

The growth trajectory of the Damaraland mole-rat is slow and continuous, ultimately reaching a definitive adult body size. Under the stable thermal regime of the burrow system, which remains near 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], an individual's ultimate wet weight plateaus at approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams]. This adult mass represents a more than tenfold increase from the 9 grams [Wwb = 9 grams] seen at birth, demonstrating the species' capacity for substantial tissue accumulation despite a low-protein diet of underground storage organs. The timing of sexual maturation is also delayed in this cooperative society. Puberty, defined as the attainment of reproductive capability, is not reached until 511 days after birth [tp = 511 days after birth], when individuals are maintained at the typical colony temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This protracted period of somatic growth before the onset of gonadal activity is a common feature in social vertebrates, where subordinate individuals delay their own reproduction to help raise the queen's offspring.

The lifespan of the Damaraland mole-rat is exceptionally long for a rodent of its mass, reflecting a slow life history pace. In captivity, where environmental contingencies are minimized, individuals have been documented to live for as long as 15.2 years [am = 15.2 years] at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This remarkable longevity is recorded under controlled conditions at a stable temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], which closely matches their natural burrow environment. The extended lifespan is linked to a very low basal metabolic rate, which reduces oxidative damage and slows the rate of physiological aging. In the wild, mortality is primarily driven by predation from snakes and small carnivores, along with infrequent stochastic events like flooding, which can collapse entire tunnel systems. Nevertheless, the potential for a 15.2-year [am = 15.2-year] lifespan provides a long window for the breeding queen to produce multiple litters and for the colony structure to persist across generations, a key element of their ecological success in the arid Kalahari regions of southern Africa at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C].
